notes.meaning: David was now about seventy years old and near the end of his life, so he appointed his son Solomon to succeed him as king. He wanted to make Solomon's kingship clear and official before any rivals could try to take the throne. God had chosen Solomon to lead the nation into peace and build the temple.

David brought together the leaders of Israel along with the priests and Levites for a national assembly. He publicly confirmed Solomon as the next king and shared the worship instructions he had received from God. Important decisions in God's kingdom were made in the open so everyone could serve together in unity.

A count was made of all Levite men who were thirty years old and older, totaling thirty-eight thousand. In Moses' day, Levites began their heavy work of carrying the tabernacle at age thirty. Now their numbers had grown greatly, providing plenty of workers for the permanent temple.

David set apart twenty-four thousand Levites to supervise the daily work of the temple, serving by turns in regular groups. Another six thousand were appointed as officers and judges across the country. These men helped local elders settle disputes and teach God's law throughout the land.

differ.view: David's musical arrangements and instruments were commanded by God through the prophets Gad and Nathan.
David introduced musical instruments into temple worship on his own initiative rather than by a direct divine command.

notes.meaning: Four thousand Levites were assigned to guard the temple gates, while another four thousand were appointed to lead music. David had designed and built special instruments for them to use in praise. Both security and music helped protect the order and reverence of worship in God's house.

notes.meaning: David divided the Levites into organized working groups based on the three sons of Levi: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. These divisions allowed the different families to take turns serving throughout the year. Serving together in family lines helped the workers encourage and support one another.

The family line of Gershom was divided into two main branches named after Ladan and Shimei. These family groups formed the basis for how the Gershonites were organized for temple duty. God kept an orderly record of each family line that served Him.

Ladan had three main descendants who led family branches: Jehiel, Zetham, and Joel. These men served as chiefs over their households during David's reign. Each leader guided his family in their shared responsibilities at the sanctuary.

Three more leaders came from another branch connected to Ladan: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran. Together with the leaders in the previous verse, they made up six family heads under Ladan. God provided capable leaders to oversee every part of the family's service.

This verse lists four family heads descending from Shimei: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. These men led their own households within the Gershonite line. Each household had a recognized place in the worship of the nation.

Jahath and Zizah had large families, but Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons. Because their numbers were small, the two smaller households were combined into one family group with a single assignment. God made sure even smaller families had an honored role without being overloaded.

Kohath, the second son of Levi, had four main sons: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. These four men founded the major clans of the Kohathites. From this branch of Levi came both the priests and many temple assistants.

Amram's sons were Aaron and Moses, but Aaron and his descendants were set apart for the priesthood forever. Their special duties were to care for the most holy things, burn incense, and pronounce God's blessing on the people. Priests served as mediators between God and the nation to lead them in prayer and sacrifice.

Moses was honored with the title man of God because the Lord had given him a special mission. Even so, his sons were not made priests but were counted as ordinary Levites. Moses showed great humility by leaving national leadership to Joshua and the priesthood to Aaron's family.

Moses had two sons named Gershom and Eliezer. Their names were constant reminders of how God had protected Moses when he was a stranger in a foreign land. Their descendants continued to serve God faithfully among the Levites without seeking special titles.

Shebuel was the chief leader among the descendants of Moses' first son, Gershom. He led his household in their assigned temple duties. Later in David's reign, leaders from this line were trusted to watch over the temple treasuries.

Eliezer had only one son, Rehabiah, who became the head of his father's house. Although Eliezer had no other sons, Rehabiah's descendants multiplied into a very large clan. God fulfilled His promise to bless Moses by giving his family many descendants to serve the sanctuary.

Shelomith was the chief descendant of Izhar, Kohath's second son. His household formed an official working unit among the Levites. Every family branch received its own recognized place in God's service.

The third son of Kohath was Hebron, whose descendants were organized under four family chiefs. These leaders were Jeriah, Amariah, Jahaziel, and Jekameam. Each of these four branches helped carry out the duties assigned to the Kohathite clan.

The fourth son of Kohath was Uzziel, whose family was led by Micah and Isshiah. These two leaders represented their households within the Levitical divisions. This completed the list of family heads descended from Kohath.

Levi's third son, Merari, had two sons named Mahli and Mushi. Mahli's line was represented in David's day by the families of Eleazar and Kish. These households made up the third major branch of temple workers.

Eleazar died having only daughters and no sons, so his family line had no male heir. In keeping with God's law for daughters who inherited property, their cousins—the sons of Kish—married them. This kept the family inheritance and service within their own clan.

The other son of Merari, Mushi, had three sons named Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth. These men served as heads of the remaining Merarite families. Their inclusion completed the official registry of Levite households.

This summary marks the close of the family list and notes that Levites were registered from twenty years of age and older. Moses had originally counted men starting at thirty, but David lowered the age to twenty. Because the nation had grown and worship would expand at the temple, more workers were needed to assist the priests.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars propose that the difference between age thirty in verse 3 and age twenty here comes from two conflicting historical sources or an ancient copying mistake.

notes.meaning: David explained that the Lord had given His people rest from their enemies and chosen Jerusalem as His permanent dwelling. Because the nation was settled in peace, the sanctuary would no longer move from place to place. True rest from God allowed His people to establish lasting, joyful worship.

Because the ark now had a permanent home, the Levites no longer needed to pack up and carry the tabernacle and its sacred furnishings. Their ancient role as physical carriers through the wilderness had come to an end. With those heavy loads gone, younger men could easily help with the daily work.

David's final instructions confirmed that Levites were to be counted for service starting at age twenty. This change was not a rash idea from his youth, but a mature decision made under God's guidance before his death. Enrolling workers at a younger age provided plenty of trained helpers for the temple.

The main duty of the Levites was to assist the priests in the daily service of God's house. They took care of the courtyards and side rooms, washed the holy dishes, and kept everything ceremonially clean. Faithful service often means doing quiet background chores so public worship can happen smoothly.

The Levites prepared the showbread, which were the twelve sacred loaves placed before God each week, along with the grain, oil, and bread for offerings. They also guarded the official measuring vessels kept at the temple. Checking these measures ensured that every offering followed God's exact standards.

Levitical musicians were assigned to stand in the temple every morning and evening to sing and play songs of thanksgiving to the Lord. This music took place alongside the daily morning and evening sacrifices. Starting and ending the day with praise reminded the people that all their time belonged to God.

The Levites helped whenever burnt offerings were presented on Sabbaths, New Moon festivals, and annual feast days. They selected, washed, and prepared the required animals so the priests could offer them on the altar. Their careful teamwork allowed large crowds of worshipers to bring their offerings without confusion.

In summary, the Levites carried out their duties for the Tent of Meeting, guarded the Holy Place, and assisted their brothers, the priests. Working in harmony under Aaron's line, they ensured that every part of temple worship was done with care. God is honored when His servants work together with mutual respect and order.
